strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses the real practical challenge that different AL strategies perform inconsistently across datasets, models, and AL cycles
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 image datasets, 3 foundation models, 20 AL cycles with 10 trials; strong empirical results (85% win rate vs. BAIT, 100% vs. SelectAL)
Solid theoretical analysis with three theorems providing formal grounding for value preservation, exponential filtering of uninformative instances, and concentration toward high-value pools
Practical utility: progressive filtering works as a standalone preprocessing step improving diverse individual strategies (+0.7% to +5.4%)
Clear, intuitive methodology that is simple to implement and ecosystem-friendly (works with existing strategies)
Extensive ablation studies examining hyperparameter sensitivity (R, α, J) and demonstrating robustness across configurations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: progressive filtering is a straightforward multi-round extension of existing single-step filtering methods (DropQuery, AlfaMix); core idea of using unions is intuitive but not particularly novel

Critical dependence on strategy ensemble composition: effectiveness depends heavily on complementary, well-performing strategies with no principled guidance for selection; acknowledged failure case (Dopanim+CLIP) when majority of strategies underperform
Problematic hyperparameter tuning: α, R, J selected on CIFAR-10 but CIFAR-10 excluded from main results, creating potential bias; no cross-dataset validation of hyperparameters
Insufficient failure analysis: Dopanim+CLIP degradation mentioned briefly but not deeply investigated; lacks analysis of what dataset/model/strategy properties predict failure modes

Theoretical limitations: bounds in Theorems 1-2 are loose and don't directly explain practical performance gains; ϵ-uninformative definition is somewhat arbitrary with no practical guidance on setting ϵ

Incomplete computational analysis: complexity stated but no wall-clock time comparisons provided; parallelization benefits mentioned but not empirically validated; memory overhead during filtering rounds not analyzed
Statistical rigor concerns: standard errors omitted 'for visibility'; no formal hypothesis testing or confidence intervals; win rate percentages lack statistical significance quantification
Limited generalization: main results on image classification only; audio use case restricted to single dataset (ESC50); no experiments on NLP, time series, or other domains

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated practical problem: AL strategy effectiveness varies across datasets/models, creating a real practitioner's dilemma
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets, 3 foundation models, 10 trials, compared against 8 individual and 3 ensemble baselines
Demonstrates practical utility: progressive filtering successfully rescues failing AL strategies (e.g., +10% for Coreset on ESC50 audio), not just ensemble wins
Thorough ablation studies systematically investigate R, α, J parameters and progressive filtering's value as preprocessing for any strategy
Clear presentation with intuitive method explanation and good visualizations (Figures 1-6)
Provides theoretical framework with three formal theorems bounding behavior of progressive filtering
weaknesses: Hyperparameter tuning bias: α=0.4, R=5, J=10 tuned on CIFAR-10 validation split, which is then excluded from main results—effectively training on data, then testing on separate data. Baseline methods not tuned per-dataset, giving REFINE unfair advantage

Limited conceptual novelty: union-based filtering is straightforward; main contribution is iterating this operation. Coverage-based selection (UHerding) already exists. Combination of existing techniques lacks fundamental innovation

Theoretical analysis doesn't justify core claims: Theorem 1 merely formalizes the obvious (union preserves highly-ranked instances). Theorem 2 assumes ϵ-uninformativeness circularly. Theorem 3 reduces to 'good strategies select good instances.' None explains why iterative filtering beats single-pass union filtering—the central claim
No comparison with single-pass union filtering: The paper never tests union-based filtering without iteration, making it impossible to validate that iteration provides value

Modest improvements without significance testing: 1-3% gains over top baselines (BAIT, UHerding) across many settings. Standard errors omitted for visibility. No statistical significance testing; with 10 trials, improvements may not be significant

Acknowledged failure mode: Dopanim+CLIP shows performance degradation when strategies perform worse than random sampling. Authors acknowledge this 'general ensemble problem' but offer only vague mitigation (future weighting schemes)

Computational overhead unquantified: M=8 strategies × J=10 × R=5 = 400 strategy evaluations per cycle vs. baselines using ~1-8. No wall-clock time comparison provided. Cost-benefit analysis missing despite showing diminishing returns at R≥5

Practical applicability limited: No principled mechanism to select complementary strategies. Authors recommend using 'well-established, complementary' strategies without guidance. Composition choice identified as critical but not systematically addressed

Limited experimental scope: All experiments on image classification except one audio example. Only frozen foundation model features tested; unclear with trainable models. Generalization beyond this setting unclear

Incomplete ablations: Limited investigation of ensemble strategy composition effects. Figure 6 validates complementary notions with only 2 strategies, not the full M=8. No testing with homogeneous strategy ensembles (all uncertainty vs. all representativeness)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine practical challenge in active learning: different strategies excel in different settings, requiring adaptive approaches rather than commitment to single strategy

Elegant and intuitive progressive filtering mechanism using iterative union-based refinement across multiple AL strategies, providing principled combination without requiring strategy selection tuning

Strong and consistent empirical results: 85-80% win rates vs. top individual strategies (BAIT, UHerding), 100% win rate vs. ensemble methods, across 6 datasets and 3 foundation models with extensive ablations

Solid theoretical analysis with three complementary theorems (value preservation, exponential reduction of uninformative instances, monotonic concentration of expected value) providing rigorous justification for the approach

Practical preprocessing utility demonstrated: progressive filtering improves any individual AL strategy (+0.7-5.4% AULC) and can fix failing strategies, enabling workflow-agnostic enhancement without abandoning existing methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with clear protocol: 20 AL cycles × 10 trials, varying dataset complexity (10-200 classes), multiple foundation models, systematic hyperparameter analysis
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, well-organized experiments, detailed algorithm descriptions, and promise of code release upon acceptance
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution combines relatively straightforward existing techniques (union-based selection, iterative refinement, coverage-based methods), representing somewhat incremental advance over existing ensemble and filtering approaches in active learning

Strong dependence on strategy ensemble composition with insufficient guidance for selection: method degrades when strategies are correlated or collectively poor (demonstrated on Dopanim/CLIP case with three strategies performing worse than random), yet paper only recommends using 'well-established, complementary strategies' without principled selection methodology

Theoretical bounds are relatively loose: probabilistic bounds may not be tight in practice, and Theorem 3's assumption that all strategies favor higher-value instances may not hold universally, with no guarantee that REFINE outperforms individual strategies

Significant computational overhead underanalyzed: requires M×J×R strategy evaluations per cycle (400 in main setup with parallelization mentioned but not evaluated); no wall-clock time comparisons provided despite potential prohibitive cost for practitioners with limited budgets

Lack of statistical significance testing: results averaged over 10 trials with standard errors omitted and some differences appearing small; confidence intervals not provided, limiting confidence in claimed improvements

Insufficient investigation of failure modes: Dopanim/CLIP degradation acknowledged but not deeply analyzed; unclear what systematic properties cause strategies to fail collectively, and whether REFINE could detect/weight strategy quality

Hyperparameter selection based on CIFAR-10 validation split with some performance variation across datasets (α=0.4 yields 6.32% on Snacks vs. 8.16% for α=0.5), raising questions about generalization despite claimed robustness
Baseline comparison concerns: SelectAL noted as having inconsistent performance and difficult to reproduce, raising fairness questions; limited comparison with recent ensemble AL methods

Limited domain generalization: primary evaluation on vision-only classification tasks with foundation models that are vision-specific; generalization to NLP, tabular data, or other modalities unclear; only one audio use case provided
Pool shrinkage mechanics underspecified: minimum pool size constraint relies on α, but no empirical analysis of pool size trajectories or how often constraint binds in practice

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real practitioner challenge of AL strategy selection variability across datasets and models

Simple, training-free progressive filtering approach with solid theoretical justification (three theorems with correct proofs on value preservation, exponential reduction of uninformative instances, and monotonic value concentration)
Comprehensive experimental validation: 6 datasets, 3 foundation models, 8 baseline strategies, 4 ensemble methods, extensive ablations, and use case study demonstrating practical utility
Consistent performance improvements: 85% win rate vs BAIT, 80% vs UHerding, 100% vs SelectAL/TAILOR; REFINE outperforms all baselines across nearly every dataset-model combination
Valuable independent contribution: progressive filtering as preprocessing improves any AL strategy (+0.7% to +5.4%), with particular benefit for weak strategies, demonstrated on audio use case
Thorough supplementary material with detailed proofs, numerical examples, robustness tests (class imbalance, distribution shift, fine-tuning), parallel timing analysis, and complete learning curves
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution (iteratively taking unions of strategy selections) is conceptually straightforward and incremental; essentially combining existing filtering and ensembling ideas
Hyperparameter selection lacks principled methodology: α=0.4, R=5, J=10 set via CIFAR-10 only with no generalizable guidance for new domains; Table 2b shows non-negligible variance across α values

Ensemble composition not systematically studied: all available strategies included without justification; Figure 10 shows performance collapse with weak majority but cause-and-effect unclear; recommendation to use 'well-established complementary strategies' is vague

Critical failure mode underexplored: Dopanim/CLIP degradation and sensitivity to weak ensemble members acknowledged but relegated to appendix; practitioners cannot easily detect these scenarios in advance

Computational overhead inadequately addressed: Table 3 shows 10:31 min acquisition at cycle 20 (comparable to training); modest 5-10% improvements may not justify 2-3× cost; only one AutoAL timing comparison provided

Theoretical limitations: Theorem 3 assumes all strategies prefer high-value instances (may not hold for biased strategies); Definition 1 (ϵ-uninformative) somewhat circular; bounds are loose with limited convergence analysis
Second-stage selection not novel: coverage-based UHerding is existing AL strategy; contribution primarily Stage 1; Figure 11 suggests Stage 2 may be less critical than claimed

Insufficient guidance on practical applicability: no principled cost-benefit analysis, no clear scenarios where REFINE outweighs computational overhead vs simpler alternatives, limited analysis of when single strong strategy suffices
Statistical significance not emphasized in main paper: Friedman tests mentioned only in Appendix E; some learning curves show overlapping error bars and modest improvements
Pool reduction aggressiveness not analyzed: Table 4 shows |C_R|/|U| from 5% to 47% across datasets with no analysis of whether more aggressive filtering is beneficial or harmful

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed experimental evaluation across 6 datasets, 3 foundation models, and extensive ablations demonstrating consistent improvements (85-100% win rates)
Clearly motivated problem addressing the practical challenge that no single AL strategy dominates across datasets and AL cycles
Progressive filtering as preprocessing step provides genuine value independent of final selection method, improving diverse AL strategies (+0.7% to +5.4%)
Solid theoretical analysis with formal proofs of value preservation, exponential reduction of uninformative instances, and monotonic improvement in expected pool value
Practical utility demonstrated through audio spectrogram use case showing ability to 'fix' failing strategies
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured methodology exposition
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: progressive filtering reduces to iterative union operations over existing strategies; coverage-based selection in stage 2 is established work (UHerding/MaxHerding); contribution is primarily engineering rather than methodological innovation
Hyperparameter tuning (R=5, J=10, α=0.4) performed on CIFAR-10 which then appears in main experiments—potential data leakage undermining generality claims across datasets

Fundamental ensemble dependency not solved: method effectiveness depends on strategy quality and complementarity; acknowledged failure case (Dopanim+CLIP) shows degradation with no principled recovery mechanism; weighting strategies proposed only as future work

Loose theoretical bounds: Theorem 1 provides weak guarantees (11% loss probability for typical settings), Theorem 2 relies on unrealistic assumption of constant low probability across all strategies/rounds, Theorem 3's key assumption may not hold early in AL; theorems characterize filtering properties but provide no performance improvement guarantees

Computational overhead inadequately analyzed: sequential acquisition costs ~10.5 min at cycle 20; no cost-per-accuracy analysis; implicit assumption computation is free; no fair equal-budget comparison with single strategies despite running 8-10 strategies per cycle

Insufficient complementarity analysis: limited to two-strategy example (Fig. 6); no systematic investigation of which combinations matter, diminishing returns, or sensitivity to removing individual strategies; design choice to use 'all available strategies' avoids harder research question

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical impact—AL strategy effectiveness varies substantially across settings, making robust strategy selection necessary
Clear and intuitive two-stage methodology with sound design rationale for core choices (union over intersection, iterative refinement, coverage-based selection)

Solid theoretical analysis with three theorems providing probabilistic bounds on value preservation, exponential filtering of uninformative instances, and concentration toward high-value pools; proofs are technically correct
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets, 3 foundation models, 8 individual + 4 ensemble baselines with 10 trials, error reporting, and pairwise win-rate analysis
Strong and consistent empirical results: 80-99% win rates vs individual strategies, 97-100% vs ensemble methods, with REFINE outperforming on majority of dataset/model combinations
Demonstrates progressive filtering as general preprocessing step improving multiple AL strategies (+0.7% to +5.4%) and enabling rescue of failing strategies (e.g., BAIT on ESC50)
Thorough ablation studies on hyperparameters (R, α, J) showing robustness across settings, and analysis of complementary notions of value
Excellent reproducibility practices: code promised, full hyperparameter specification, extensive supplementary material with proofs and additional experiments
Honest discussion of limitations including explicit acknowledgment of failure case when ensemble contains weak strategies
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: theorems represent straightforward probability bounds (union bounds for Theorem 1, repeated filtering for Theorem 2) rather than deep insights; theoretical contributions are correct but expected

Fundamental limitation with weak ensemble problem not resolved: performance degrades when majority of strategies underperform (Dopanim/CLIP case), yet recommended strategy is to 'use all available'—no principled way to avoid or detect this a priori

Hyperparameter selection (α=0.4, R=5, J=10) tuned on CIFAR-10 and excluded from main results, introducing subtle bias toward that dataset's characteristics; no theoretical guidance for setting hyperparameters across different problems

Design choices lacking thorough justification: why union over weighted voting with learned thresholds? Coverage-based stage 2 appears interchangeable with simpler alternatives (Figure 11 shows FIR/EER comparable), suggesting this stage may be less critical

Incomplete analysis of strategy complementarity: Figure 6 demonstrates one pair (Margin + TypiClust) but no systematic investigation of which strategy combinations are synergistic or how to select complementary ensembles

Aggressive filtering with risk of data loss: Table 4 shows CIFAR-10 retains only 5.2% of pool (95% removal)—while theoretically bounded, empirical risk of removing valuable instances; behavior highly dataset-dependent (5.2% to 100% retention)

Computational overhead: sequential acquisition times of 9-10 minutes per cycle (Table 3) substantial for practitioners without parallelization; AutoAL comparison shows REFINE is parallelizable but slower sequentially than some alternatives

Empirical improvements sometimes modest: error bands overlap between REFINE and top baselines (especially UHerding) on several datasets in Figure 3; win-rate aggregation can obscure case-by-case variability

Comparison fairness concerns: unclear if all ensemble baselines use identical M=8 strategy sets as REFINE; SelectAL noted as difficult to reproduce, potentially unfair comparison; large gap to oracle (BoSS) suggests fundamental algorithmic limitations remain
Presentation issues: important content in appendix (proofs, audio experiments); limited upfront discussion of failure modes; limited guidance on when to use vs. not use REFINE
